title: Universities, scholarships and research partnerships: keeping UK engagement effective
label: 13 October 2026 · Higher education and research partnerships
summary: The Committee questioned UK higher-education representatives about the value of British universities' international work, the damage done by recent funding cuts and visa restrictions, and how future policy should balance scholarships, long-term ODA research partnerships, private finance and research security to support development and UK interests. Witnesses argued for sustained multi-year funding, localisation of research leadership, smarter visa exemptions for vetted scholars, careful use of private capital, expanded transnational education, and stronger, pragmatic links between universities and government.

speakers.label: Harry Anderson
speakers.name: Harry Anderson
speakers.role: Deputy Director for Policy and Global Engagement, Universities UK International

glossary.definition: Official Development Assistance – Government money spent to support development in poorer countries.
Global Challenges Research Fund – a UK research fund (2016–2021) that backed international development research and partnerships.
Strategic Partnerships for Higher Education Innovation and Reform – a UK programme funding university partnerships in developing countries.
Transnational education – UK higher-education provision delivered overseas, for example by branch campuses or validated local courses.
A UK government scholarship programme for international students, usually one-year masters scholarships.
A UK body that funds research scholarships (masters and PhDs) for candidates from Commonwealth countries.
Antimicrobial resistance – when bacteria and other microbes stop responding to medicines, a global health threat.
British International Investment – the UK’s development finance institution that makes investments in developing countries.
Research Collaboration Advice Panel – government advice and support for UK research institutions about sensitive international partnerships.

chapters.title: Who was speaking and why it matters
chapters.takeaway: IDS and Universities UK International described universities as key development infrastructure: they teach, build local research capacity and create long-lasting diplomatic ties through scholarships and partnerships.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We are looking at higher education and research partnerships the UK supports; please introduce yourselves briefly and say what your organisations do internationally.

turns.speaker: Professor Anuradha Joshi
turns.text: I run the Institute of Development Studies (IDS) at Sussex: we’re a research institute with masters programmes, focused on applied development problems and training people who go on to work in policy and practice in the global south.

turns.speaker: Harry Anderson
turns.text: I’m deputy director at Universities UK International, which represents 142 UK universities; we push that universities are critical development infrastructure—they teach, research and build long-term partnerships abroad.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: So you both see universities as not just commercial exporters but institutions that strengthen countries and create ties important to UK foreign policy.

turns.speaker: Professor Anuradha Joshi
turns.text: Exactly—students and researchers trained in the UK or on UK programmes often stay in-country but use UK methods and networks, and those relationships matter when those people later hold influence.

chapters.title: Scholarships, visas and soft power
chapters.takeaway: Commonwealth and Chevening scholarships are high-value soft power tools, but recent cuts and visa restrictions are damaging UK reputation and blocking talented students from coming.

turns.speaker: Dr Sam Rushworth
turns.text: You’ve seen reductions in some scholarship programmes. What does that look like on the ground for research and country influence?

turns.speaker: Professor Anuradha Joshi
turns.text: Cuts and visa brakes have immediate effects: IDS went from 24 funded scholars in 2025–26 to seven this year because some countries were blocked, and that undermines our teaching and networks.

turns.speaker: David Mundell
turns.text: Do you have evidence that scholarship alumni stay and contribute back home, or do lots leave for better jobs elsewhere?

turns.speaker: Professor Anuradha Joshi
turns.text: Many alumni are motivated to return; institutions track this and embassies follow up. We can provide reports showing alumni impact—people who go on to influential public or private roles.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: On visa policy: could some students—Chevening or Commonwealth scholars—have been exempted? Was the blanket approach necessary?

turns.speaker: Harry Anderson
turns.text: The visa brake damaged perceptions of the UK as a reliable partner. A targeted exemption for vetted scholarship recipients would have preserved commitments and saved reputational damage.

turns.speaker: Monica Harding
turns.text: Where else will students go if they can’t come to the UK?

turns.speaker: Professor Anuradha Joshi
turns.text: Some will take offers in Europe, Australia or other English-speaking options—but language, quality and fit vary; losing the UK option is a big loss for many.

chapters.title: What good ODA-funded research partnerships do
chapters.takeaway: Long-term, locally owned ODA-funded partnerships build trust, train researchers in-country, and produce practical policy changes that short-term projects or private investors usually can't achieve.

turns.speaker: James Naish
turns.text: With GCRF and SPHEIR gone or cut, what is lost? How should successors be designed?

turns.speaker: Professor Anuradha Joshi
turns.text: GCRF and earlier programmes funded networks, early-stage translational research, and training. A successor needs sustained funding, local ownership, and linkages between research and teaching.

turns.speaker: Harry Anderson
turns.text: Universities want a successor with a multi-year funding envelope, clear priorities and enough time to rebuild trust with partners, otherwise short projects just won’t deliver systemic change.

turns.speaker: Dr Sam Rushworth
turns.text: Are there low-cost models to build research capacity?

turns.speaker: Professor Anuradha Joshi
turns.text: Yes: IDS’s multi-methods course trained thousands of African mid-career researchers; initial external funding seeded a programme that local cohorts then sustained—replicable and high impact.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: So the focus should be on localisation: local researchers leading agendas and long-term mentoring, not brief UK-led projects.

chapters.title: Private finance and transnational education
chapters.takeaway: Private capital and transnational education (TNE) can help but won’t replace public ODA; TNE offers a major opportunity to scale education in-country, provided quality and local development goals are central.

turns.speaker: Tracy Gilbert
turns.text: The Government looks to private investment to fill ODA gaps—what are the risks for development research?

turns.speaker: Harry Anderson
turns.text: Private capital can catalyse projects and scale innovations, but it tends to chase monetisable returns and specific geographies; public funding must remain for public goods and early-stage risk-taking.

turns.speaker: Professor Anuradha Joshi
turns.text: Agreed—private finance won’t fund many public goods, like certain health services or orphan crops; regulation and public oversight are essential to avoid inequitable outcomes.

turns.speaker: James Naish
turns.text: How should the UK use the large TNE footprint—hundreds of thousands studying for UK awards overseas—as part of development policy?

turns.speaker: Harry Anderson
turns.text: TNE is now a major channel: almost 700,000 students study for UK degrees overseas. If aligned to local skills needs and quality assured, TNE can build capacity in-country without driving brain drain.

turns.speaker: Professor Anuradha Joshi
turns.text: Linking TNE to research partnerships gives a two-way benefit: students learn from research and bring it into their countries, while research gains local insight and continuity.

chapters.title: Security, university finances and practical asks of government
chapters.takeaway: Universities face genuine research-security risks and financial pressures; they want clearer, long-term government engagement, smart visa exemptions, and protection for vulnerable students and academic freedoms.

turns.speaker: James Naish
turns.text: Universities have faced warnings about foreign influence. How are you managing research security and partnerships—do we need stricter controls?

turns.speaker: Harry Anderson
turns.text: Universities take security seriously: we’ve strengthened due diligence, supported the Research Collaboration Advice Panel and an academic-interference reporting route; but we must balance openness, research freedom and safety.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Do universities have the capacity to spot covert risks, and are you asking for more government support?

turns.speaker: Harry Anderson
turns.text: We’ve made progress—ATAS expanded, MI5 has engaged vice-chancellors—but universities need resources and coherent government channels to coordinate security, export control and diplomacy.

turns.speaker: David Mundell
turns.text: What about financial strain on universities and the knock-on effect on international partnerships?

turns.speaker: Harry Anderson
turns.text: The sector is under acute financial pressure; international student income now underpins many institutions. That fragility reduces universities’ ability to sustain overseas partnerships—longer-term public funding would help.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Final quick asks: one line each—are your voices heard in government and what do you need most?

turns.speaker: Professor Anuradha Joshi
turns.text: We have influence but need clearer, long-term funding streams and better recognition of universities as development infrastructure.

turns.speaker: Harry Anderson
turns.text: We want joined-up government engagement, visa flexibility for vetted scholars, and sustained multi-year funding to rebuild trust with partners.
